text: June, 1893. A young Indian lawyer is sitting in a first class compartment on a train in
South Africa. He has a valid ticket. A white passenger complains. At Peter Meritsberg
station, he is thrown off the train. He spent that night shivering in the station waiting
room, deciding whether to go home or to fight. He stayed and fought for more than 20 years.
years. His name was Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi. When he came home to India in 1915, people
would come to call him Mahatma, great soul. His weapon was Satyagraha, holding on to the
truth and resisting without violence. In 1919, in Amritsar, thousands of people gathered
peacefully in a walled garden called Jallianwala Bagh. A British general blocked the exit
and ordered his troops to fire into the crowd. They fired until they ran out of bullets. The
official count was 379 dead. Indian estimates were over a thousand. After Amritsar, millions
of Indians who had trusted the British stopped trusting them. And Gandhi chose the most unlikely
weapon in history. Remember that Indian cloth? Remember Manchester? Gandhi told Indians to
burn foreign cloth and spin their own. He sat at a spinning wheel, the charka, every day
and wore rough homespun cotton called kadi. The spinning wheel went onto the freedom movement's
flag. The cloth that had once made India rich would now help set it free. In 1930 he picked
an even stranger target, salt. The British taxed it and Indians were banned from making
their own. So Gandhi walked to the sea. Mr. Gandhi, what exactly are you doing? Picking up salt.
That's illegal. Then arrest me and the thousands behind me.
Looking at the crowd, then his notebook. I'll need a bigger notebook.
